Take-Home_Ex02

Author

JUNCHEN LI

Published

May 29, 2026

Modified

June 4, 2026

1 Introduction

1.1 Background

Tenant Thread operates through a multi-agent environment in which employees, personal agents, office systems, and external platforms interact through a large number of automated events. These interactions include email access, file access, task delegation, calendar scheduling, advice generation, and public posting activities.

The key incident examined in this report is an anomalous post sent to SaidIT by John Windward on May 17, 2046, at approximately 4:21 AM. The incident raises an important operational question: was the post caused by a single isolated mistake, or was it the visible outcome of a broader failure pattern within the multi-agent system?

Rather than treating the anomalous post as an isolated text-quality issue, this report reconstructs the underlying event chain. The analysis examines how instructions, files, people, agents, and systems interacted before the post was released. It also compares the latest incident with earlier suspicious behaviours to identify whether similar warning signals appeared previously.

1.2 Investigation Objective

The purpose of this report is to use visual analytics to trace the origin and propagation of the anomalous SaidIT post. The analysis focuses on four objectives:

  1. Reconstruct the exact sequence of events that led to the public post.
  2. Identify the people, agents, files, and systems involved in the event chain.
  3. Compare the latest incident with earlier suspicious behaviours.
  4. Recommend one targeted intervention point that could reduce the likelihood of recurrence.

1.3 Analytical Questions

This report addresses the following questions:

  • How was the anomalous SaidIT post generated?
  • Which people, personal agents, and systems were involved?
  • What was the confirmed content source of the post?
  • Did similar suspicious behaviours occur before the latest incident?
  • Where should the system intervene to prevent similar public releases?

2 Getting Started

2.1 Analytical Approach

This investigation follows a staged visual analytics workflow. The first stage prepares and audits the raw JSON data. The second stage extracts suspicious instruction-file handoffs. The third stage reconstructs the latest incident and compares it with earlier suspicious chains. The final stage evaluates a targeted intervention point.

This staged approach is important because the event log contains nested and heterogeneous records. Different event types contain different detail fields. Therefore, the analysis preserves the original JSON structure first and only extracts selected fields when they are needed for a specific analytical purpose.

2.2 Analytical Tools

The analysis is conducted in R using Quarto for reproducible reporting. The main packages support the following tasks:

  • jsonlite imports the raw JSON files.
  • tidyverse supports data cleaning, transformation, and visualisation.
  • lubridate standardises Unix timestamps and local time.
  • DT creates searchable interactive tables.
  • plotly supports interactive visual analytics.
  • igraph, tidygraph, and ggraph support network analysis.
if (!requireNamespace("pacman", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pacman")
}

pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  jsonlite,
  lubridate,
  janitor,
  scales,
  DT,
  plotly,
  igraph,
  ggraph,
  tidygraph
)

theme_set(theme_minimal())

2.3 Data Sources

The investigation uses two JSON files.

  • MC2 data.json contains the internal event timeline. Each record represents an action performed by a person, personal agent, office system, or external platform.
  • org_chart.json contains the Tenant Thread organization structure, including departments, teams, people, and reporting relationships.

Before importing the data, the current project folder is checked to confirm that both JSON files are available.

3 Data Preparation and Quality Control

3.1 Importing the Raw JSON Files

The two JSON files are imported without simplifying nested structures. This choice is deliberate. The event log contains a details object whose structure changes across event types. For example, a file-access event may store a file path, while a task-delegation event may store a target agent and a nested task argument.

To avoid losing information during import, the original nested structure is preserved. The raw objects are retained throughout the analysis so that later derived tables can always be traced back to the original records.

mc2_raw <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  "data/MC2/MC2 data.json",
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)

org_raw <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  "data/MC2/org_chart.json",
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)

3.2Inspecting the Top-Level Structure

The top-level structure is inspected before any transformation is performed. This step confirms whether the expected components are present and provides a basic audit of the available records.

For the event log, the main object should contain a description and an ordered list of events. For the organization chart, the main object should contain nodes and edges. The number of events, nodes, and edges is also recorded to establish the initial scale of the dataset.

names(mc2_raw)
[1] "description" "events"     
names(org_raw)
[1] "directed"   "multigraph" "graph"      "nodes"      "edges"     
length(mc2_raw$events)
[1] 185147
length(org_raw$nodes)
[1] 75
length(org_raw$edges)
[1] 74

3.3 Creating the Raw Event Table

The event records are converted into a tibble with five core variables:

  • id: the unique event identifier;
  • short_name: the action performed;
  • when: the original Unix timestamp;
  • parties: the people, agents, or systems involved;
  • details: additional nested information associated with the event.

The parties and details variables are intentionally retained as list-columns. This preserves the original event structure and avoids prematurely flattening fields that may not exist for every event type.

events_raw <- tibble(
  id = map_int(mc2_raw$events, ~ .x$id),
  short_name = map_chr(mc2_raw$events, ~ .x$short_name),
  when = map_dbl(mc2_raw$events, ~ .x$when),
  parties = map(mc2_raw$events, ~ .x$parties),
  details = map(mc2_raw$events, ~ .x$details)
)

3.4 Standardising Timestamp Variables

The raw when variable is stored as a Unix timestamp. To support reproducible sequence analysis, the timestamps are converted into both UTC time and local time.

UTC time is retained as the standard reference. Local time is created using the America/Los_Angeles time zone because the incident description refers to an anomalous SaidIT post sent at approximately 4:21 AM local time.

The analysis also creates date-level and hour-level variables. These variables will later support timeline visualisations, historical comparisons, and incident-window filtering.

events_clean <- events_raw %>%
  mutate(
    timestamp_utc = as_datetime(
      when,
      tz = "UTC"
    ),
    timestamp_local = with_tz(
      timestamp_utc,
      tzone = "America/Los_Angeles"
    ),
    event_date_local = as_date(
      timestamp_local
    ),
    event_hour_local = floor_date(
      timestamp_local,
      unit = "hour"
    ),
    party_count = map_int(
      parties,
      length
    )
  )

3.5 Reviewing the Available Time Range

The time range is checked before further analysis. This step verifies that the imported records cover the key incident period and identifies whether the dataset includes historical and post-incident events.

event_time_range <- events_clean %>%
  summarise(
    earliest_event_utc = min(
      timestamp_utc,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    latest_event_utc = max(
      timestamp_utc,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    earliest_event_local = min(
      timestamp_local,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    latest_event_local = max(
      timestamp_local,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    number_of_days = as.numeric(
      difftime(
        max(timestamp_local, na.rm = TRUE),
        min(timestamp_local, na.rm = TRUE),
        units = "days"
      )
    )
  )

event_time_range

3.6 Defining the Key Incident Time

The investigation is anchored around the anomalous SaidIT post sent on May 17, 2046, at approximately 4:21 AM local time.

A dedicated incident-time object is created so that all later filters use a consistent reference point.

incident_time_local <- ymd_hms(
  "2046-05-17 04:21:00",
  tz = "America/Los_Angeles"
)

incident_time_utc <- with_tz(
  incident_time_local,
  tzone = "UTC"
)

incident_time_local
[1] "2046-05-17 04:21:00 PDT"
incident_time_utc
[1] "2046-05-17 11:21:00 UTC"

3.7 Auditing Event Data Quality

Before analysing suspicious behaviours, the event table is checked for structural problems.

The audit focuses on:

  • duplicated event IDs;
  • missing event IDs;
  • missing action names;
  • missing timestamps;
  • events without listed parties;
  • invalid party counts.

These checks are important because missing timestamps or duplicated IDs could distort event ordering and inflate interaction counts.

event_quality_summary <- events_clean %>%
  summarise(
    total_events = n(),
    unique_event_ids = n_distinct(id),
    duplicate_event_ids = n() - n_distinct(id),
    missing_event_ids = sum(is.na(id)),
    missing_short_names = sum(is.na(short_name)),
    missing_timestamps = sum(is.na(timestamp_utc)),
    empty_parties = sum(party_count == 0),
    minimum_party_count = min(
      party_count,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    maximum_party_count = max(
      party_count,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

event_quality_summary

1       185147           185147                   0                 0

3.8 Identifying Duplicate Event IDs

A separate duplicate check is created so that repeated event identifiers can be reviewed directly.

duplicate_event_ids <- events_clean %>%
  count(
    id,
    name = "record_count"
  ) %>%
  filter(
    record_count > 1
  )

duplicate_event_ids
# A tibble: 0 × 2
# ℹ 2 variables: id <int>, record_count <int>

3.9 Reviewing Event Types

The distribution of event types provides an initial view of how the multi-agent system operates.

This summary helps distinguish routine actions, such as email access and file reading, from incident-relevant activities, such as subordinate-task delegation, file deletion, SaidIT post checks, and public posting events.

event_type_summary <- events_clean %>%
  count(
    short_name,
    sort = TRUE
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    event_share = n / sum(n)
  )

3.11 Interactive Event-Type Table

A searchable table is included to support further exploration of all event types.

DT::datatable(
  event_type_summary %>%
    mutate(
      event_share = percent(
        event_share,
        accuracy = 0.01
      )
    ),
  options = list(
    pageLength = 15,
    scrollX = TRUE
  ),
  rownames = FALSE
)

3.12 Inspecting the Immediate Incident Window

An initial incident window is created to inspect events occurring shortly before and shortly after the anomalous post.

This narrow window is useful for identifying the final actions that occurred immediately before public release. The full propagation chain will be reconstructed in a later section.

incident_window_5min <- events_clean %>%
  filter(
    timestamp_local >= incident_time_local - minutes(5),
    timestamp_local <= incident_time_local + minutes(5)
  ) %>%
  select(
    id,
    timestamp_local,
    short_name,
    parties,
    details
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    timestamp_local,
    id
  )

    timestamp_local <= incident_time_local + minutes(5)
  ) %>%
  select(
    id,
    timestamp_local,
    short_name,
    parties,
    details
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    timestamp_local,
    id
  )

3.14 Reviewing Incident-Relevant Event Types

The following filter checks whether SaidIT-related events and file-deletion events appear in the imported dataset.

incident_relevant_event_types <- events_clean %>%
  filter(
    str_detect(
      short_name,
      regex(
        "saidit|post|delete_file|queue_subordinate_task",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  count(
    short_name,
    sort = TRUE
  )

NoteOutput Warning

The first two phases establish a reproducible analytical foundation.

The raw JSON objects are preserved, event records are converted into a structured table, timestamps are standardised, and core quality-control checks are completed. The event-type review and incident-window inspection provide the first view of the system activity surrounding the anomalous SaidIT post.

The next phase will expand party-level records, normalise actor names, and identify which people, agents, and systems appear most frequently in the event log.
